The Brown deer mouse (Peromyscus megalops) is a relatively large-bodied member of its genus, with adult females attaining a maximum wet body weight of approximately 66 grams [Wwi = approximately 66 grams], a mass that places it among the heavier Peromyscus species. Females typically produce litters of six pups [N_R_i = litters of six pups] and can sustain up to three and a half such litters annually [F_R_i = up to three and a half such litters annually] under the favorable thermal conditions of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], yielding a substantial reproductive output for a murid rodent of this size. Neonates emerge from the birth canal weighing roughly 2.9 grams [Wwb = roughly 2.9 grams], a modest birth mass that underscores the altricial nature of the newborn. This initial investment is low relative to the ultimate maternal mass, reflecting a strategy of producing relatively small, rapidly developing offspring. The species' comparatively large adult size is believed to support its occupation of higher-elevation forest habitats, where cooler temperatures and seasonal resource pulses place a premium on the capacity to store reserves and sustain prolonged gestation.

Gestation in Peromyscus megalops proceeds for an average period of 22.8 days [tg = 22.8 days] when the female is maintained at a core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a duration that aligns closely with the gestation lengths documented in related cotton mice. Following parturition, the altricial neonates enter a suckling stage and remain dependent on maternal milk for approximately 22 days [tx = approximately 22 days], completing the pre-weaning phase at this same thermal regime of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. The weaning period marks the onset of nutritional independence, after which the young begin to forage for solid food items such as seeds and arthropods. This comparatively short lactation interval is characteristic of the genus and facilitates a rapid turnover of generations, allowing females to invest in multiple litters within a single breeding season. The direct coupling of gestation and lactation durations with maternal body temperature highlights the tight physiological integration of reproductive timing with the endothermic capacity of this species.

Puberty, defined by the attainment of full reproductive maturity, occurs at approximately 58 days after birth [tp = approximately 58 days after birth] under the same stable thermal conditions of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This relatively early maturation enables young born early in the spring to contribute to the breeding population within the same season, a demographic trait that can drive rapid population growth under favorable environmental conditions. The age at which first oestrus is observed is consistent with the reproductive schedules of many temperate cricetid rodents, though it is somewhat accelerated compared to larger-bodied forest mice. The post-weaning period thus represents a critical window during which juveniles must acquire sufficient body reserves to support the energetic demands of gonadal development and the initiation of reproductive activity. Field studies suggest that the timing of puberty may be modulated by food availability and population density, with individuals in resource-rich years maturing slightly earlier than those in years of scarcity.

Basal metabolic rate in the Brown deer mouse has been measured at 90.64 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 90.64 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when the animal is resting within its thermoneutral zone at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This rate is a reflection of the species' relatively large body size compared to other members of the genus, as oxygen consumption scales predictably with mass among endotherms. The elevated metabolic demands associated with maintaining a 66 gram [Wwi = 66 gram] adult body mass are likely supported by a diet rich in high-energy seeds, fungi, and invertebrates, which are abundant in the forested highlands of its range. Respirometry trials conducted on captive individuals show that the metabolic rate is sensitive to ambient temperature, with oxygen consumption increasing below the thermoneutral zone as thermoregulatory costs rise. These data contribute to a broader understanding of how body size and thermal physiology interact to shape the energetic niche of montane Peromyscus species.

Maximum longevity in Peromyscus megalops has been recorded at approximately 912 days [am = approximately 912 days] under controlled conditions maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], though wild individuals likely experience considerably shorter lifespans due to predation and environmental stressors. This lifespan, equivalent to about two and a half years, is typical for a rodent of this body size and reproductive tempo, reflecting a life history strategy that balances high annual reproductive output against a relatively brief period of reproductive opportunity. Mortality in the field is most pronounced during the first weaning transition, when newly independent juveniles must navigate unfamiliar terrain and evade predators without the protection of the maternal burrow. Among adults, reproductive senescence has been observed in females beyond their second breeding season, with litter sizes declining noticeably. The interplay between a moderate lifespan and a high intrinsic rate of increase positions the Brown deer mouse as a resilient species capable of withstanding seasonal fluctuations in resource availability within its mountain forest habitat.
